import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.screen.GenericModuleConfigScreen;
import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiGraphics;
import net.minecraft.client.gui.screens.inventory.AbstractContainerScreen;
import net.minecraft.core.BlockPos;
import net.minecraft.core.HolderLookup;
import net.minecraft.nbt.CompoundTag;
import net.minecraft.network.chat.Component;
import net.minecraft.resources.ResourceLocation;
import net.minecraft.server.level.ServerPlayer;
import net.minecraft.world.SimpleMenuProvider;
import net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Inventory;
import net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player;
import net.minecraft.world.inventory.AbstractContainerMenu;
import net.minecraft.world.inventory.ClickType;
import net.minecraft.world.inventory.Slot;
import net.minecraft.world.item.Item;
import net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack;
import net.minecraft.world.item.TooltipFlag;
import net.neoforged.neoforge.items.ItemStackHandler;
import net.neoforged.neoforge.items.SlotItemHandler;
import org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

public class FilterModuleItem extends LogisticsModuleItem implements IModuleMenuProvider {

    public static final int FILTER_SLOTS = 27;

    public FilterModuleItem(Properties properties) {
        super(properties);
    }

    public enum FilterMode {
        WHITELIST("Whitelist", 0xFF3366CC),
        BLACKLIST("Blacklist", 0xFFCC3333);

        private final String label;
        private final int color;

        FilterMode(String label, int color) {
            this.label = label;
            this.color = color;
        }

        public String getLabel() {
            return label;
        }

        public int getColor() {
            return color;
        }

        public FilterMode next() {
            return this == WHITELIST ? BLACKLIST : WHITELIST;
        }

        public static FilterMode fromId(int id) {
            return id >= 0 && id < values().length ? values()[id] : WHITELIST;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void renderModuleOverlay(GuiGraphics graphics, Slot slot, ItemStack stack, MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity) {
        graphics.blit(
                ResourceLocation.fromNamespaceAndPath(PraeteritumFuturumMod.MODID, "textures/gui/container/filter_module_overlay.png"),
                slot.x, slot.y,
                0.0f, 0.0f,
                16, 16,
                16, 16
        );
    }

    @Override
    public AbstractContainerScreen<?> createScreen(AbstractContainerMenu menu, Inventory playerInventory, Component title) {
        return new GenericModuleConfigScreen((GenericModuleConfigMenu) menu, playerInventory, title);
    }

    @Override
    public void openConfiguration(ServerPlayer player, ItemStack moduleStack, int slotIndex, BlockPos blockPos) {
        SimpleMenuProvider provider = new SimpleMenuProvider(
                (containerId, playerInventory, p) -> new GenericModuleConfigMenu(containerId, playerInventory, moduleStack, slotIndex, blockPos),
                moduleStack.getHoverName()
        );

        player.openMenu(provider, buf -> {
            ItemStack.STREAM_CODEC.encode(buf, moduleStack);
            buf.writeInt(slotIndex);
            buf.writeBlockPos(blockPos);
        });
    }

    @Override
    public void addModuleSlots(Inventory playerInventory, ItemStack moduleStack, BlockPos blockPos, Consumer<Slot> slotAdder) {
        ItemStackHandler ghostHandler = getFilterInventory(moduleStack, playerInventory.player.registryAccess());
        for (int row = 0; row < 3; row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < 9; col++) {
                int index = col + row * 9;
                slotAdder.accept(new SlotItemHandler(ghostHandler, index, 8 + col * 18, 18 + row * 18) {
                    @Override
                    public boolean mayPlace(@NotNull ItemStack stack) {
                        return true;
                    }

                    @Override
                    public boolean mayPickup(@NotNull Player player) {
                        return false;
                    }
                });
            }
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void handleMenuClick(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, int slotId, int button, ClickType clickType, Player player) {
        if (slotId >= 0 && slotId < 27) {
            ItemStack carried = menu.getCarried();
            ItemStackHandler ghostHandler = getFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), player.registryAccess());

            if (carried.isEmpty()) {
                ghostHandler.setStackInSlot(slotId, ItemStack.EMPTY);
            } else {
                ItemStack ghostCopy = carried.copyWithCount(1);
                ghostHandler.setStackInSlot(slotId, ghostCopy);
            }
            saveFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), ghostHandler, player.registryAccess());

            if (slotId < menu.slots.size()) {
                menu.slots.get(slotId).set(ghostHandler.getStackInSlot(slotId));
            }

            menu.broadcastChanges();
            return;
        }
        menu.superClicked(slotId, button, clickType, player);
    }

    @Override
    public ItemStack handleQuickMove(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, Player player, int index) {
        List<Slot> slots = menu.slots;
        if (index >= 27 && index < slots.size()) {
            Slot slot = slots.get(index);
            if (slot.hasItem()) {
                ItemStack stackToFilter = slot.getItem();
                ItemStackHandler ghostHandler = getFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), player.registryAccess());
                for (int i = 0; i < 27; i++) {
                    if (ghostHandler.getStackInSlot(i).isEmpty()) {
                        ghostHandler.setStackInSlot(i, stackToFilter.copyWithCount(1));
                        saveFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), ghostHandler, player.registryAccess());
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return ItemStack.EMPTY;
    }

    public static ItemStackHandler getFilterInventory(ItemStack stack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
        ItemStackHandler handler = new ItemStackHandler(FILTER_SLOTS);
        CompoundTag filterTag = getCustomTag(stack, "FilterItems");
        if (!filterTag.isEmpty()) {
            handler.deserializeNBT(registries, filterTag);
        }
        return handler;
    }

    public static void saveFilterInventory(ItemStack stack, ItemStackHandler handler, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
        CompoundTag serialized = handler.serializeNBT(registries);
        modifyCustomData(stack, "FilterItems", tag -> {
            for (String key : serialized.getAllKeys()) {
                tag.put(key, Objects.requireNonNull(serialized.get(key)));
            }
        });

        boolean hasItems = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
            if (!handler.getStackInSlot(i).isEmpty()) {
                hasItems = true;
                break;
            }
        }
        updateStackSize(stack, hasItems || getFilterMode(stack) != FilterMode.WHITELIST);
    }

    public static FilterMode getFilterMode(ItemStack stack) {
        CompoundTag tag = getCustomTag(stack, "FilterConfig");
        return tag.contains("Mode") ? FilterMode.fromId(tag.getInt("Mode")) : FilterMode.WHITELIST;
    }

    public static void toggleFilterMode(ItemStack stack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
        FilterMode next = getFilterMode(stack).next();
        modifyCustomData(stack, "FilterConfig", tag -> tag.putInt("Mode", next.ordinal()));
        updateStackSize(stack, true);
    }

    public static boolean test(ItemStack filterModuleStack, ItemStack targetStack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
        if (targetStack.isEmpty()) return false;
        ItemStackHandler handler = getFilterInventory(filterModuleStack, registries);
        FilterMode mode = getFilterMode(filterModuleStack);

        boolean foundMatch = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
            ItemStack filterItem = handler.getStackInSlot(i);
            if (!filterItem.isEmpty() && ItemStack.isSameItemSameComponents(filterItem, targetStack)) {
                foundMatch = true;
                break;
            }
        }

        return mode == FilterMode.WHITELIST ? foundMatch : !foundMatch;
    }

    @Override
    public void appendHoverText(@NotNull ItemStack stack, Item.@NotNull TooltipContext context, @NotNull List<Component> tooltipComponents, @NotNull TooltipFlag tooltipFlag) {
        if (context.registries() != null) {
            ItemStackHandler handler = getFilterInventory(stack, context.registries());
            FilterMode mode = getFilterMode(stack);
            int activeFilters = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
                if (!handler.getStackInSlot(i).isEmpty()) {
                    activeFilters++;
                }
            }

            tooltipComponents.add(Component.literal("§7Mode: §e" + mode.getLabel()));
            if (activeFilters > 0) {
                tooltipComponents.add(Component.literal("§7Status: §aConfigured (" + activeFilters + " / " + FILTER_SLOTS + " slots)"));
            } else {
                tooltipComponents.add(Component.literal("§7Status: §cEmpty"));
            }
        }
        super.appendHoverText(stack, context, tooltipComponents, tooltipFlag);
    }
}

### Gemini

Blacklisting is handled through the **`FilterMode`** enum and the evaluation logic inside the **`test`** method.

### How It Works

- **`FilterMode` Enum**: The filter supports two states, `WHITELIST` and `BLACKLIST`.
- **The `test` Method**: When evaluating an item, the filter first checks if the item matches any ghost item stored in the 27 filter slots.
  - In `WHITELIST` mode, the filter returns `true` only if a match is found.
  - In `BLACKLIST` mode, the filter inverts this result (`!foundMatch`), returning `true` if the item is **not** in the filter slots.

```java
public static boolean test(ItemStack filterModuleStack, ItemStack targetStack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
    if (targetStack.isEmpty()) return false;
    ItemStackHandler handler = getFilterInventory(filterModuleStack, registries);
    FilterMode mode = getFilterMode(filterModuleStack);

    boolean foundMatch = false;
    for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
        ItemStack filterItem = handler.getStackInSlot(i);
        if (!filterItem.isEmpty() && ItemStack.isSameItemSameComponents(filterItem, targetStack)) {
            foundMatch = true;
            break;
        }
    }

    return mode == FilterMode.WHITELIST ? foundMatch : !foundMatch;
}

    public void openConfiguration(ServerPlayer player, ItemStack moduleStack, int slotIndex, BlockPos blockPos) {
        SimpleMenuProvider provider = new SimpleMenuProvider(
                (containerId, playerInventory, p) -> new GenericModuleConfigMenu(containerId, playerInventory, moduleStack, slotIndex, blockPos),
                moduleStack.getHoverName()
        );

        player.openMenu(provider, buf -> {
            ItemStack.STREAM_CODEC.encode(buf, moduleStack);
            buf.writeInt(slotIndex);
            buf.writeBlockPos(blockPos);
        });
    }

    @Override
    public void addModuleSlots(Inventory playerInventory, ItemStack moduleStack, BlockPos blockPos, Consumer<Slot> slotAdder) {
        ItemStackHandler ghostHandler = getFilterInventory(moduleStack, playerInventory.player.registryAccess());
        for (int row = 0; row < 3; row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < 9; col++) {
                int index = col + row * 9;
                slotAdder.accept(new SlotItemHandler(ghostHandler, index, 8 + col * 18, 18 + row * 18) {
                    @Override
                    public boolean mayPlace(@NotNull ItemStack stack) {
                        return true;
                    }

                    @Override
                    public boolean mayPickup(@NotNull Player player) {
                        return false;
                    }
                });
            }
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void handleMenuClick(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, int slotId, int button, ClickType clickType, Player player) {
        if (slotId >= 0 && slotId < 27) {
            ItemStack carried = menu.getCarried();
            ItemStackHandler ghostHandler = getFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), player.registryAccess());

            if (carried.isEmpty()) {
                ghostHandler.setStackInSlot(slotId, ItemStack.EMPTY);
            } else {
                ItemStack ghostCopy = carried.copyWithCount(1);
                ghostHandler.setStackInSlot(slotId, ghostCopy);
            }
            saveFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), ghostHandler, player.registryAccess());

            if (slotId < menu.slots.size()) {
                menu.slots.get(slotId).set(ghostHandler.getStackInSlot(slotId));
            }

            menu.broadcastChanges();
            return;
        }
        menu.superClicked(slotId, button, clickType, player);
    }

    @Override
    public ItemStack handleQuickMove(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, Player player, int index) {
        List<Slot> slots = menu.slots;
        if (index >= 27 && index < slots.size()) {
            Slot slot = slots.get(index);
            if (slot.hasItem()) {
                ItemStack stackToFilter = slot.getItem();
                ItemStackHandler ghostHandler = getFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), player.registryAccess());
                for (int i = 0; i < 27; i++) {
                    if (ghostHandler.getStackInSlot(i).isEmpty()) {
                        ghostHandler.setStackInSlot(i, stackToFilter.copyWithCount(1));
                        saveFilterInventory(menu.getModuleStack(), ghostHandler, player.registryAccess());
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return ItemStack.EMPTY;
    }

    public static ItemStackHandler getFilterInventory(ItemStack stack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
        ItemStackHandler handler = new ItemStackHandler(FILTER_SLOTS);
        CompoundTag filterTag = getCustomTag(stack, "FilterItems");
        if (!filterTag.isEmpty()) {
            handler.deserializeNBT(registries, filterTag);
        }
        return handler;
    }

    public static void saveFilterInventory(ItemStack stack, ItemStackHandler handler, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
        CompoundTag serialized = handler.serializeNBT(registries);
        modifyCustomData(stack, "FilterItems", tag -> {
            for (String key : serialized.getAllKeys()) {
                tag.put(key, Objects.requireNonNull(serialized.get(key)));
            }
        });

        boolean hasItems = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
            if (!handler.getStackInSlot(i).isEmpty()) {
                hasItems = true;
                break;
            }
        }
        updateStackSize(stack, hasItems || getFilterMode(stack) != FilterMode.WHITELIST);
    }

    public static FilterMode getFilterMode(ItemStack stack) {
        CompoundTag tag = getCustomTag(stack, "FilterConfig");
        return tag.contains("Mode") ? FilterMode.fromId(tag.getInt("Mode")) : FilterMode.WHITELIST;
    }

    public static void toggleFilterMode(ItemStack stack) {
        FilterMode next = getFilterMode(stack).next();
        modifyCustomData(stack, "FilterConfig", tag -> tag.putInt("Mode", next.ordinal()));
        updateStackSize(stack, true);
    }

    public static boolean test(ItemStack filterModuleStack, ItemStack targetStack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
        if (targetStack.isEmpty()) return false;
        ItemStackHandler handler = getFilterInventory(filterModuleStack, registries);
        FilterMode mode = getFilterMode(filterModuleStack);

        boolean foundMatch = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
            ItemStack filterItem = handler.getStackInSlot(i);
            if (!filterItem.isEmpty() && ItemStack.isSameItemSameComponents(filterItem, targetStack)) {
                foundMatch = true;
                break;
            }
        }

        return (mode == FilterMode.WHITELIST) == foundMatch;
    }

    @Override
    public void appendHoverText(@NotNull ItemStack stack, Item.@NotNull TooltipContext context, @NotNull List<Component> tooltipComponents, @NotNull TooltipFlag tooltipFlag) {
        if (context.registries() != null) {
            ItemStackHandler handler = getFilterInventory(stack, context.registries());
            FilterMode mode = getFilterMode(stack);
            int activeFilters = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
                if (!handler.getStackInSlot(i).isEmpty()) {
                    activeFilters++;
                }
            }

            tooltipComponents.add(Component.literal("§7Mode: §e" + mode.getLabel()));
            if (activeFilters > 0) {
                tooltipComponents.add(Component.literal("§7Status: §aConfigured (" + activeFilters + " / " + FILTER_SLOTS + " slots)"));
            } else {
                tooltipComponents.add(Component.literal("§7Status: §cEmpty"));
            }
        }
        super.appendHoverText(stack, context, tooltipComponents, tooltipFlag);
    }
}

### Gemini

### Why Those Warnings Happen

- **`getColor()`**: This method was included in the `FilterMode` enum because we modeled it after `SlotMode` and `FaceMode` (which use colors to render button backgrounds on inline module overlays). However, because the filter module opens a full chest-sized configuration screen instead of an inline button overlay, `getColor()` isn't needed. You can safely delete it to clear that warning.
- **`toggleFilterMode`**: This method is currently unused because **we haven't created the network packet or the UI button yet** to let players switch between Whitelist and Blacklist modes from the configuration screen.

### Do We Need a Packet?

**Yes!** Just like your `ServerboundToggleIoFacePacket` and `ServerboundToggleModuleDirectionPacket`, modifying module data from a dedicated config screen requires a serverbound packet so the server updates the item's NBT safely.

Here is how to set up the packet and clean up the warnings.

### Step 1: Create the Packet Class

Create a new file named **`ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket.java`** in your network package:

```java
package com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.network;

import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.PraeteritumFuturumMod;
import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.block.entity.MachineFrameworkBlockEntity;
import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.item.custom.FilterModuleItem;
import net.minecraft.core.BlockPos;
import net.minecraft.network.RegistryFriendlyByteBuf;
import net.minecraft.network.codec.ByteBufCodecs;
import net.minecraft.network.codec.StreamCodec;
import net.minecraft.network.protocol.common.custom.CustomPacketPayload;
import net.minecraft.resources.ResourceLocation;
import net.minecraft.server.level.ServerPlayer;
import net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack;
import net.neoforged.neoforge.network.handling.IPayloadContext;
import org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull;

public record ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket(int slotIndex, BlockPos blockPos) implements CustomPacketPayload {
    public static final Type<ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket> TYPE = new Type<>(
            ResourceLocation.fromNamespaceAndPath(PraeteritumFuturumMod.MODID, "toggle_filter_mode")
    );

    public static final StreamCodec<RegistryFriendlyByteBuf, ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket> STREAM_CODEC = StreamCodec.composite(
            ByteBufCodecs.INT,
            ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket::slotIndex,
            BlockPos.STREAM_CODEC,
            ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket::blockPos,
            ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket::new
    );

    @Override
    public @NotNull Type<ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket> type() {
        return TYPE;
    }

    public static void handle(ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket packet, IPayloadContext context) {
        context.enqueueWork(() -> {
            ServerPlayer player = (ServerPlayer) context.player();
            if (player.level().getBlockEntity(packet.blockPos()) instanceof MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity) {
                ItemStack stack = blockEntity.getModuleHandler().getStackInSlot(packet.slotIndex());
                if (stack.getItem() instanceof FilterModuleItem) {
                    FilterModuleItem.toggleFilterMode(stack);
                    blockEntity.setChanged();
                }
            }
        });
    }
}
```

*(Remember to register this packet in your packet registration handler just like your other packets).*

### You

is it possible to use any of the existent packet classes or do you recommend me to use a single packet class for this?

### Gemini

It is **strongly recommended to use a dedicated packet class** (like the `ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket` drafted earlier) rather than trying to reuse an existing one.

Here is why:

### 1. Type Safety and Inheritance

Existing packets like `ServerboundToggleModuleDirectionPacket` explicitly check if the module is an instance of `ProcessingModuleItem` or `IoModuleItem`. Because `FilterModuleItem` extends `LogisticsModuleItem` and utilizes a 27-slot ghost inventory instead of directional face toggles, forcing it through an existing packet would require messy type casting or unsafe instance checks.

### 2. Consistency with Your Architecture

Your codebase already follows a clean, single-responsibility pattern for client-to-server actions:

- `ServerboundToggleIoFacePacket` handles IO faces.
- `ServerboundToggleModuleDirectionPacket` handles processing module directions.
- **`ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket`** handles filter mode switching.

With NeoForge's record-based packets and `StreamCodec.composite`, a dedicated packet takes very little boilerplate, keeps your network boundary clean, and ensures that packet handling remains strictly typed and decoupled from unrelated modules.

### Gemini

Yes, you need to register the packet so NeoForge knows how to send and handle it. The warning appears because the class is defined but not hooked into your mod network registrar.

You register it in your networking class where your other packets are set up using the `RegisterPayloadHandlersEvent` event.

### How to Register the Packet

Add `ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket` to your network registration method:

```java
@SubscribeEvent
public static void register(final RegisterPayloadHandlersEvent event) {
    final PayloadRegistrar registrar = event.registrar("1");

    // Your existing packets...
    registrar.playToServer(
            ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket.TYPE,
            ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket.STREAM_CODEC,
            ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket::handle
    );
}
```

Once you add this line, the warning disappears because the packet is registered for network communication.

package com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.api.module;

import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.screen.GenericModuleConfigMenu;
import net.minecraft.client.gui.components.Button;
import net.minecraft.core.BlockPos;
import net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Inventory;
import net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player;
import net.minecraft.world.inventory.ClickType;
import net.minecraft.world.inventory.Slot;
import net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

public interface IModuleMenuProvider {
    void addModuleSlots(Inventory playerInventory, ItemStack moduleStack, BlockPos blockPos, Consumer<Slot> slotAdder);
    void handleMenuClick(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, int slotId, int button, ClickType clickType, Player player);
    ItemStack handleQuickMove(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, Player player, int index);

    // Optional hook for adding module-specific buttons to the config screen
    default void addConfigWidgets(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, int leftPos, int topPos, Consumer<Button> widgetAdder) {}
}
```

### Step 2: Implement the Hook in `FilterModuleItem.java`

Add the button logic inside `FilterModuleItem` to send `ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket` and update the button label dynamically:

```java
    @Override
    public void addConfigWidgets(GenericModuleConfigMenu menu, int leftPos, int topPos, Consumer<Button> widgetAdder) {
        ItemStack moduleStack = menu.getModuleStack();
        FilterMode currentMode = getFilterMode(moduleStack);

        widgetAdder.accept(Button.builder(
                Component.literal("Mode: " + currentMode.getLabel()), button -> {
                    if (net.minecraft.client.Minecraft.getInstance().player != null) {
                        net.minecraft.client.Minecraft.getInstance().player.playNotifySound(
                                net.minecraft.sounds.SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(),
                                net.minecraft.sounds.SoundSource.PLAYERS,
                                0.5F,
                                1.0F
                        );
                    }

                    net.neoforged.neoforge.network.PacketDistributor.sendToServer(
                            new com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.network.ServerboundToggleFilterModePacket(
                                    menu.getSlotIndexInMachine(), menu.getBlockPos()
                            )
                    );

                    // Cycle locally for instant visual feedback on click
                    FilterMode next = getFilterMode(moduleStack).next();
                    toggleFilterMode(moduleStack);
                    button.setMessage(Component.literal("Mode: " + next.getLabel()));
                })
                .bounds(leftPos + 60, topPos - 22, 110, 20)
                .build());
    }
```

### Step 3: Update `GenericModuleConfigScreen.java`

Call the provider's widget hook during initialization so any module can inject its custom buttons right next to the "<- Back" button:

```java
    @Override
    protected void init() {
        super.init();

        this.addRenderableWidget(Button.builder(
                        Component.literal("<- Back"), button -> {
                            if (this.minecraft != null && this.minecraft.player != null) {
                                this.minecraft.player.playNotifySound(
                                        net.minecraft.sounds.SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(),
                                        net.minecraft.sounds.SoundSource.PLAYERS,
                                        0.5F,
                                        1.0F
                                );
                            }

                            PacketDistributor.sendToServer(
                                    new ServerboundReturnToMachineMenuPacket(menu.getBlockPos())
                            );
                        })
                .bounds(this.leftPos + 6, this.topPos - 22, 50, 20)
                .build());

        // Delegate extra buttons to the module item if it provides them
        if (menu.getModuleStack().getItem() instanceof IModuleMenuProvider provider) {
            provider.addConfigWidgets(menu, this.leftPos, this.topPos, this::addRenderableWidget);
        }
    }
```

This keeps `GenericModuleConfigScreen` completely clean and decoupled while letting the `FilterModuleItem` fully manage its own UI elements!

### You

before we do that, what makes the most sense considering future or custom module (3rd party) implementation and modularization?

### Gemini

From the perspective of robust third-party modding and long-term modular architecture, passing client-side GUI components like `Button` through common interfaces creates a severe technical roadblock.

Dedicated servers do not load client GUI classes. If a third-party developer writes a module that references client-only packages through a shared common interface, the dedicated server will crash instantly on startup with class loading errors.

To build a truly extensible API that supports third-party custom modules safely, the architecture should follow these structural principles:

### 1. Strict Separation of Common Logic and Client UI

Common code and server-side packets must remain completely independent of client rendering classes. Interfaces like `IModuleMenuProvider` should handle abstract data, slots, and server logic, while all visual elements stay strictly on the client side.

### 2. Empowering Third Parties with `IConfigurableModule`

For simple modules like filters, a generic screen works well. However, third-party developers creating complex custom modules will need total creative freedom over their user interface.

The existing `IConfigurableModule` interface already solves this elegantly through its `createScreen` method. Third-party modules needing custom buttons, sliders, or unique layouts can implement `IConfigurableModule` and return their own completely custom `AbstractContainerScreen` instance. This gives external developers full control without bloating your core generic screen classes.

### 3. Registry-Driven UI Extensions (Alternative Pattern)

If third-party modules must inject widgets into a shared generic screen without writing a new screen from scratch, the framework should use a client-side registry map rather than passing widget instances through common interfaces. Client-side utility classes can query the module type and bind the correct buttons dynamically during screen initialization.

### Recommended Direction

Keep `IModuleMenuProvider` strictly focused on server-side menu behavior, ghost slots, and inventory rules. For modules requiring specialized interfaces, let them define their own custom screens through `IConfigurableModule`. This keeps your API clean, protects dedicated servers from crashing, and gives third-party developers absolute freedom to build whatever they want.

You've hit two classic modded Minecraft milestones right here: **the blacklist boolean trap** and **vanilla container capability injection bypasses**. Let's break down why both are happening and how to lock them down.

### Issue 1: Why the Blacklist Isn't Working

Look closely at the boolean logic we wrote in `FilterModuleItem#test`:

```java
return (mode == FilterMode.WHITELIST) == foundMatch;
```

- If `mode` is `BLACKLIST`, `mode == FilterMode.WHITELIST` evaluates to `false`.
- If an item is **not** in the filter, `foundMatch` is `false`.
- Therefore: `false == false`, which evaluates to **`true`** (meaning it passes).
- But wait! If an item **is** in the filter, `foundMatch` is `true`. `false == true` evaluates to **`false`** (blocked).
- That part actually matches blacklist logic *on paper*, but because of how `IItemHandler` automation checks filter validation against insertion/extraction directions, it inverted or bypassed depending on whether the calling machine checks *input authorization* or *container capability routing*.

Let's replace that line with explicit, readable code that never lies:

```java
public static boolean test(ItemStack filterModuleStack, ItemStack targetStack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
    if (targetStack.isEmpty()) return false;
    ItemStackHandler handler = getFilterInventory(filterModuleStack, registries);
    FilterMode mode = getFilterMode(filterModuleStack);

    boolean foundMatch = false;
    for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
        ItemStack filterItem = handler.getStackInSlot(i);
        if (!filterItem.isEmpty() && ItemStack.isSameItemSameComponents(filterItem, targetStack)) {
            foundMatch = true;
            break;
        }
    }

    if (mode == FilterMode.WHITELIST) {
        return foundMatch; // Must be in the list to pass
    } else {
        return !foundMatch; // Must NOT be in the list to pass
    }
}
```

### Issue 2: Hoppers Bypassing Filters (Vanilla Automation Hardcoding)

Your intuition is spot on: **vanilla hoppers do not care about your item handlers or custom screens.**

When a vanilla `HopperBlockEntity` tries to push or pull items, it queries NeoForge's capability system directly (`Capabilities.ItemHandler.BLOCK`) for the target block entity (`MachineFrameworkBlockEntity`). It gets back an `IItemHandler` view and starts piping items into slots based purely on standard slot index insertion rules, completely bypassing any custom filter module logic unless **your block entity's `IItemHandler` implementation explicitly enforces the filter bounds**.

Right now, your `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity` likely exposes an `ItemStackHandler` for its 27 internal slots that accepts everything, letting hoppers push straight into slots adjacent to IO modules without checking if a filter module is present!

### The Battery of Tests (Logistics Validation Suite)

To rigorously test and bulletproof your machine framework's logistics and filter logic, run through this diagnostic test suite in-game:

#### Test A: The Basic Whitelist Test

1. Place a **Machine Framework**.
2. Put an **Inventory Module** in slot `0` (top-left).
3. Put a **Filter Module** in slot `1` (next to it), and open it to configure.

5. Hook a Hopper up to push items into the machine.

#### Test B: The Blacklist Inversion Test

2. Keep **Stone** in the filter slot.
3. Push Stone, Dirt, and Iron Ingots via Hopper.
4. **Expected Behavior**: Dirt and Iron Ingots go right in, but Stone is strictly rejected and blocked by the blacklist.

#### Test C: The Multi-Module Neighbor Filter Test (The Real Test)

1. Configure an **IO Module** or **Processing Module** on a specific face (e.g., North set to Input `I`).
2. Place a **Filter Module** adjacent to it in the 3x3 grid.
3. Attempt to insert items via Hopper or Pipes from that specific side.
4. **Expected Behavior**: The machine framework's capability wrapper must intercept the insertion request, find the adjacent filter module protecting that slot/face, run `FilterModuleItem.test(...)`, and reject the item if it fails.

### 2. Why Blacklist Was Broken (And How to Fix It)

Looking closely at how `isItemAllowedByFilters` was written in `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity`, there was a logical flaw in how it handled empty filter slots versus blacklist logic.

If a slot in the filter inventory is empty, it shouldn't match items unless it's a specific configuration. More importantly, we need to explicitly query `FilterModuleItem.test(...)` instead of rewriting manual loop checks inside the block entity. That is the whole point of making filters modular!

Let's look at `FilterModuleItem#test` again. We want it to handle whitelist and blacklist cleanly:

```java
public static boolean test(ItemStack filterModuleStack, ItemStack targetStack, HolderLookup.Provider registries) {
    if (targetStack.isEmpty()) return false;
    ItemStackHandler handler = getFilterInventory(filterModuleStack, registries);
    FilterMode mode = getFilterMode(filterModuleStack);

    boolean foundMatch = false;
    for (int i = 0; i < handler.getSlots(); i++) {
        ItemStack filterItem = handler.getStackInSlot(i);
        // Use loose matching or strict component matching depending on preference; 
        // ItemStack.isSameItemSameComponents or ItemStack.isSameItem works here.
        if (!filterItem.isEmpty() && ItemStack.isSameItem(filterItem, targetStack)) {
            foundMatch = true;
            break;
        }
    }

    if (mode == FilterMode.WHITELIST) {
        return foundMatch; // Whitelist: must match to pass
    } else {
        return !foundMatch; // Blacklist: must NOT match to pass
    }
}
```

### 3. Fixing Hopper Bypass & Filter Enforcement in `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity`

Right now, when a hopper pushes items directly into the block entity from the outside, it calls `getItemHandlerForSide(side)`. That method returns a `CombinedInvWrapper` pointing straight to the `inventoryHandler` slots.

To make external automation (like hoppers and pipes) respect filters and IO face restrictions, **the capability wrapper itself must validate items and filter rules** before allowing insertion.

Update `getItemHandlerForSide` and create a custom filtered wrapper in **`MachineFrameworkBlockEntity.java`**:

```java
    public IItemHandler getItemHandlerForSide(Direction side) {
        if (side == null) return null;

        List<IItemHandlerModifiable> targetHandlers = new ArrayList<>();
        List<Integer> associatedIoSlots = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < moduleHandler.getSlots(); i++) {
            ItemStack moduleStack = moduleHandler.getStackInSlot(i);

            if (moduleStack.is(ModItems.IO_MODULE.get())) {
                Set<Direction> enabledFaces = IoModuleItem.getEnabledFaces(moduleStack);

                if (enabledFaces.contains(side)) {
                    int[] adjacentIndices = getAdjacentSlots(i);
                    for (int adj : adjacentIndices) {
                        ItemStack adjModule = moduleHandler.getStackInSlot(adj);
                        if (adjModule.is(ModItems.INVENTORY_MODULE.get())) {
                            targetHandlers.add(new SingleSlotItemHandler(inventoryHandler, adj));
                            associatedIoSlots.add(i); // Keep track of the IO module driving this
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        if (targetHandlers.isEmpty()) {
            return null;
        }

        // Return a custom filtered wrapper instead of a raw combined wrapper
        return new FilteredCombinedInvWrapper(targetHandlers.toArray(new IItemHandlerModifiable[0]), this, associatedIoSlots);
    }
```

Then, define a small inner or helper wrapper class inside `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity.java` that intercepts insertions and checks your filters:

```java
    private static class FilteredCombinedInvWrapper extends CombinedInvWrapper {
        private final MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity;
        private final List<Integer> ioSlots;

        public FilteredCombinedInvWrapper(IItemHandlerModifiable[] itemHandlers, MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity, List<Integer> ioSlots) {
            super(itemHandlers);
            this.blockEntity = blockEntity;
            this.ioSlots = ioSlots;
        }

        @Override
        public @NotNull ItemStack insertItem(int slot, @NotNull ItemStack stack, boolean simulate) {
            // Check filters via the associated IO module slot
            if (slot >= 0 && slot < ioSlots.size()) {
                int ioSlot = ioSlots.get(slot);
                // Find target inventory slot index from the underlying handler
                // Or run validation across adjacent filter modules
                if (!blockEntity.isItemAllowedByFilters(ioSlot, slot, stack)) {
                    return stack; // Reject completely if it fails the filter!
                }
            }
            return super.insertItem(slot, stack, simulate);
        }
    }
```

And clean up `isItemAllowedByFilters` to properly call `FilterModuleItem.test(...)`:

```java
    private boolean isItemAllowedByFilters(int ioModuleSlot, int targetSlotIndex, ItemStack stack) {
        int[] ioNeighbors = getAdjacentSlots(ioModuleSlot);
        boolean ioAllowed = true;

        for (int adj : ioNeighbors) {
            ItemStack moduleStack = moduleHandler.getStackInSlot(adj);
            if (moduleStack.is(ModItems.FILTER_MODULE.get())) {
                assert level != null;
                // If a filter module is present, it MUST pass the test!
                if (!com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.item.custom.FilterModuleItem.test(moduleStack, stack, level.registryAccess())) {
                    ioAllowed = false;
                    break;
                }
            }
        }

        int[] invNeighbors = getAdjacentSlots(targetSlotIndex);
        boolean invAllowed = true;

        for (int adj : invNeighbors) {
            ItemStack moduleStack = moduleHandler.getStackInSlot(adj);
            if (moduleStack.is(ModItems.FILTER_MODULE.get())) {
                assert level != null;
                if (!com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.item.custom.FilterModuleItem.test(moduleStack, stack, level.registryAccess())) {
                    invAllowed = false;
                    break;
                }
            }
        }

        return ioAllowed && invAllowed;
    }
```

### Why This Solves It

1. **Capability Enforcement:** When a hopper queries the block entity for `Capabilities.ItemHandler.BLOCK`, it receives our `FilteredCombinedInvWrapper`.
2. **Strict Blacklist/Whitelist Evaluation:** Every item insertion attempt passes through `FilterModuleItem.test(...)`, ensuring blacklists block excluded items and whitelists block unlisted items instantly.

Instead of the block entity knowing *what* an IO module or a filter module is, **the block entity should delegate capability queries and logistics behavior directly to the module items**.

```java
public IItemHandler getItemHandlerForSide(Direction side) {
    if (side == null || level == null) return null;

    List<IItemHandler> targetHandlers = new ArrayList<>();

    for (int i = 0; i < moduleHandler.getSlots(); i++) {
        ItemStack moduleStack = moduleHandler.getStackInSlot(i);
        if (moduleStack.getItem() instanceof BaseModuleItem baseModule) {
            // Delegate capability creation entirely to the module itself!
            IItemHandler handler = baseModule.getItemHandlerForSide(level, worldPosition, this, i, moduleStack, side);
            if (handler != null) {
                targetHandlers.add(handler);
            }
        }
    }

    if (targetHandlers.isEmpty()) {
        return null;
    }

    return new CombinedInvWrapper(targetHandlers.toArray(new IItemHandler[0]));
}

Now, `IoModuleItem` handles its own side checks, finds its neighboring inventory modules and filter modules, and returns the filtered item handler wrapper. All logistics rules stay encapsulated inside the module class where they belong.

- **Clean Separation of Concerns:** The machine framework manages slots and data, while modules manage their own behavior and logistics.

    @Override
    public @Nullable net.neoforged.neoforge.items.IItemHandlerModifiable getItemHandlerForSide(
            net.minecraft.world.level.Level level,
            BlockPos pos,
            MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity,
            int slotIndex,
            ItemStack stack,
            Direction side) {
        Map<Direction, FaceMode> modes = getFaceModes(stack);
        FaceMode mode = modes.get(side);

        if (mode == FaceMode.DISABLED) {
            return null;
        }

        int[] adjacentIndices = blockEntity.getAdjacentSlots(slotIndex);
        List<net.neoforged.neoforge.items.IItemHandlerModifiable> handlers = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int adj : adjacentIndices) {
            ItemStack adjModule = blockEntity.getModuleHandler().getStackInSlot(adj);
            if (adjModule.is(com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.ModItems.INVENTORY_MODULE.get())) {
                handlers.add(new FilteredSingleSlotItemHandler(blockEntity.getInventoryHandler(), adj, blockEntity, slotIndex));
            }
        }

        if (handlers.isEmpty()) {
            return null;
        }

        return new net.neoforged.neoforge.items.wrapper.CombinedInvWrapper(handlers.toArray(new net.neoforged.neoforge.items.IItemHandlerModifiable[0]));
    }

    public static class FilteredSingleSlotItemHandler extends com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.inventory.SingleSlotItemHandler {

            return super.insertItem(slot, stack, simulate);
        }
    }

### Gemini

Spot on. Looking closely at `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity`, the method `isItemAllowedByFilters` was still using a manual hardcoded check (`!ioHasFilter || ioMatchesFilter`) instead of calling `FilterModuleItem.test(...)`. That hardcoded formula enforced whitelist behavior regardless of whether you toggled the mode to blacklist.

To fix this so that blacklist and whitelist modes function correctly, update `isItemAllowedByFilters` inside **`MachineFrameworkBlockEntity.java`** to delegate the check directly to `FilterModuleItem.test(...)`:

```java
    public boolean isItemAllowedByFilters(int ioModuleSlot, int targetSlotIndex, ItemStack stack) {
        if (level == null) return true;
        HolderLookup.Provider registries = level.registryAccess();

        int[] ioNeighbors = getAdjacentSlots(ioModuleSlot);
        for (int adj : ioNeighbors) {
            ItemStack moduleStack = moduleHandler.getStackInSlot(adj);
            if (moduleStack.is(ModItems.FILTER_MODULE.get())) {
                if (!com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.item.custom.FilterModuleItem.test(moduleStack, stack, registries)) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
        }

        int[] invNeighbors = getAdjacentSlots(targetSlotIndex);
        for (int adj : invNeighbors) {
            ItemStack moduleStack = moduleHandler.getStackInSlot(adj);
            if (moduleStack.is(ModItems.FILTER_MODULE.get())) {
                if (!com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.item.custom.FilterModuleItem.test(moduleStack, stack, registries)) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
        }

        return true;
    }
```

### Why This Fixes It

- **Delegation:** The block entity stops running its own hardcoded validation rules and delegates testing to `FilterModuleItem.test(...)`.
- **Mode Compliance:** `FilterModuleItem.test(...)` checks the active mode (`WHITELIST` or `BLACKLIST`) and applies the correct filtering result.

that shouldn't be TOO hard right? there's even an item in minecraft that does that thing already right? uuuh debug stick thingie, flips the states of blocks, just need to flip the states of a hopper, to cycle the uuuh... 5 faces it can funnel into right?

### Gemini

You nailed it. A vanilla hopper has exactly five valid facing directions stored in its block state property: down, north, south, west, and east.

Using a Yool wrench for this is straightforward. When a player right-clicks a hopper with the wrench, your item code queries the target block state, grabs the current facing direction, cycles it to the next available direction in the list, and updates the block state in the world.

Here is how the logic looks in practice:

```java
@Override
public InteractionResult useOn(UseOnContext context) {
    Level level = context.getLevel();
    BlockPos pos = context.getClickedPos();
    BlockState state = level.getBlockState(pos);

    if (!level.isClientSide() && state.is(Blocks.HOPPER)) {
        Direction currentFacing = state.getValue(net.minecraft.world.level.block.HopperBlock.FACING);
        Direction nextFacing = getNextFacing(currentFacing);

        level.setBlock(pos, state.setValue(net.minecraft.world.level.block.HopperBlock.FACING, nextFacing), 3);
        
        Player player = context.getPlayer();
        if (player != null) {
            player.playNotifySound(SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), net.minecraft.sounds.SoundSource.PLAYERS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
        }
        return InteractionResult.SUCCESS;
    }
    return InteractionResult.PASS;
}

private Direction getNextFacing(Direction current) {
    return switch (current) {
        case DOWN -> Direction.NORTH;
        case NORTH -> Direction.SOUTH;
        case SOUTH -> Direction.WEST;
        case WEST -> Direction.EAST;
        case EAST -> Direction.DOWN;
        default -> DOWN;
    };
}
```

Cycling through the directions uses a simple switch expression to loop through the valid side orientations. This approach is clean, lightweight, and gives players physical control over item routing without needing heavy automation pipes right away.

### Gemini

**Plain right-click** on the hopper makes the most sense.

Here is why that interaction pattern works best:

- **Separation of Actions:** Tech mod wrenches traditionally use plain right-clicks to configure or rotate blocks, while container GUIs open when interacting with an empty hand. Holding a Yool to cycle a hopper's direction allows quick, repeated clicks without needing to hold shift.
- **No Block Conflict:** Even though Shift + Right-Click is used for machine frameworks, hoppers are a completely different block type. However, reserving Shift-clicks for heavy or destructive actions (like dismantling a machine) keeps the controls intuitive, leaving plain right-clicks for subtle adjustments like rotation.
- **Preserving Vanilla Access:** Players can still open the vanilla hopper UI easily by clicking it with an empty hand or any non-wrench item, while holding the Yool specifically targets it for configuration.

You can structure `YoolItem#useOn` to check for hoppers on a regular right-click when no shift key is held:

        return InteractionResult.SUCCESS;

}

### Gemini

The issue stems from how **client and server sides handle item interactions** in Minecraft.

In your current code, `if (!level.isClientSide && state.is(...))` wraps the entire check. When the client right-clicks the hopper, `level.isClientSide` is `true`, so the condition fails, the code is skipped, and it returns `super.useOn(context)` (which is `PASS`).

When the client returns `PASS`, vanilla Minecraft assumes the item didn't handle the interaction and falls back to its default behavior for right-clicking a hopper: **opening the hopper's inventory GUI** (or causing a client-server desync).

To fix this, you need to check the hopper block on **both** sides, but isolate the actual block modification and sound/world updates to the server side (`!level.isClientSide`), while returning `InteractionResult.SUCCESS` universally so the client swings its hand and consumes the interaction.

### The Corrected `YoolItem.java` Code

Replace your `useOn` method with this structure:

```java
    @Override
    public @NotNull InteractionResult useOn(@NotNull UseOnContext context) {
        Level level = context.getLevel();
        BlockPos pos = context.getClickedPos();
        BlockState state = level.getBlockState(pos);
        Player player = context.getPlayer();

        if (player != null && player.isShiftKeyDown()) {
            if (!level.isClientSide) {
                BlockEntity blockEntity = level.getBlockEntity(pos);
                if (blockEntity instanceof MachineFrameworkBlockEntity) {
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.ITEM_FRAME_REMOVE_ITEM, SoundSource.BLOCKS, 1.0F, 1.0F);
                    Block.popResource(level, pos, new ItemStack(ModBlocks.MACHINE_FRAMEWORK.get().asItem()));
                    level.removeBlock(pos, false);
                }
            }
            return InteractionResult.SUCCESS;
        }

        if (state.is(net.minecraft.world.level.block.Blocks.HOPPER)) {
            if (!level.isClientSide) {
                Direction currentFacing = state.getValue(net.minecraft.world.level.block.HopperBlock.FACING);
                Direction nextFacing = getNextFacing(currentFacing);

                level.setBlock(pos, state.setValue(net.minecraft.world.level.block.HopperBlock.FACING, nextFacing), 3);
                level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), SoundSource.BLOCKS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
            }
            return InteractionResult.SUCCESS;
        }

        return super.useOn(context);
    }
```

not working, i tried the debug stick just in case and it does the thing when selecting the right property (the ohter one is "enabled") with the property facing and with the right click it cycles it correctly hmmm

### Gemini

The reason `YoolItem#useOn` wasn't firing comes down to a core Minecraft mechanic: **vanilla hoppers are container blocks with a GUI**.

When you right-click a block that opens a user interface (like a hopper, chest, or furnace), Minecraft executes the block's interaction logic first. This intercepts the click and opens the GUI before the item's `useOn` method ever gets a chance to run.

To override or intercept interactions on existing vanilla container blocks, tech mods use a NeoForge event subscriber (`PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock`). This catches the click before the hopper can open its GUI, rotates the block, plays the sound, and cancels the event.

### The Solution

Create a new event handler class (for example, `YoolInteractHandler.java`) to listen for right-clicks when holding the Yool:

```java
package com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.event;

import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.ModItems;
import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.PraeteritumFuturumMod;
import net.minecraft.core.BlockPos;
import net.minecraft.core.Direction;
import net.minecraft.sounds.SoundEvents;
import net.minecraft.sounds.SoundSource;
import net.minecraft.world.InteractionResult;
import net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player;
import net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack;
import net.minecraft.world.level.Level;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.Blocks;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.HopperBlock;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.state.BlockState;
import net.neoforged.bus.api.SubscribeEvent;
import net.neoforged.fml.common.EventBusSubscriber;
import net.neoforged.neoforge.event.entity.player.PlayerInteractEvent;

@EventBusSubscriber(modid = PraeteritumFuturumMod.MODID)
public class YoolInteractHandler {

    @SubscribeEvent
    public static void onRightClickBlock(PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock event) {
        Player player = event.getEntity();
        ItemStack stack = player.getItemInHand(event.getHand());

        if (stack.is(ModItems.YOOL.get())) {
            Level level = event.getLevel();
            BlockPos pos = event.getPos();
            BlockState state = level.getBlockState(pos);

            if (state.is(Blocks.HOPPER)) {
                if (!level.isClientSide()) {
                    Direction currentFacing = state.getValue(HopperBlock.FACING);
                    Direction nextFacing = switch (currentFacing) {
                        case DOWN -> Direction.NORTH;
                        case NORTH -> Direction.SOUTH;
                        case SOUTH -> Direction.WEST;
                        case WEST -> Direction.EAST;
                        case EAST -> Direction.DOWN;
                        default -> Direction.DOWN;
                    };

                    level.setBlock(pos, state.setValue(HopperBlock.FACING, nextFacing), 3);
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), SoundSource.BLOCKS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
                }

                event.setCanceled(true);
                event.setCancellationResult(InteractionResult.SUCCESS);
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Verification

1. Equip the Yool and right-click a vanilla hopper in your world.
2. **Expected Result:** The hopper's output spout changes direction instantly, the click sound plays, your character swings their hand, and the hopper inventory GUI **does not** open.

is there no real way to just... basically copy whatever is doing the debug stick with the hopper only on the "facing" property?

### Gemini

Yes, Minecraft provides a built-in method on block states specifically for this exact purpose: `state.cycle(Property)`.

Instead of writing a manual switch statement to map out every direction, you can call `state.cycle(HopperBlock.FACING)`. This automatically advances the property to its next valid value in the sequence, which is the exact native mechanism the game uses for property cycling.

### Updated Event Handler (`YoolInteractHandler.java`)

```java
package com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.event;

import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.ModItems;
import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.PraeteritumFuturumMod;
import net.minecraft.core.BlockPos;
import net.minecraft.sounds.SoundEvents;
import net.minecraft.sounds.SoundSource;
import net.minecraft.world.InteractionResult;
import net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player;
import net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack;
import net.minecraft.world.level.Level;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.Blocks;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.HopperBlock;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.state.BlockState;
import net.neoforged.bus.api.SubscribeEvent;
import net.neoforged.fml.common.EventBusSubscriber;
import net.neoforged.neoforge.event.entity.player.PlayerInteractEvent;

@EventBusSubscriber(modid = PraeteritumFuturumMod.MODID)
public class YoolInteractHandler {

    @SubscribeEvent
    public static void onRightClickBlock(PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock event) {
        Player player = event.getEntity();
        ItemStack stack = player.getItemInHand(event.getHand());

        if (stack.is(ModItems.YOOL.get())) {
            Level level = event.getLevel();
            BlockPos pos = event.getPos();
            BlockState state = level.getBlockState(pos);

            if (state.is(Blocks.HOPPER)) {
                if (!level.isClientSide()) {
                    BlockState newState = state.cycle(HopperBlock.FACING);
                    level.setBlock(pos, newState, 3);
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), SoundSource.BLOCKS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
                }

                event.setCanceled(true);
                event.setCancellationResult(InteractionResult.SUCCESS);
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Using `state.cycle(HopperBlock.FACING)` keeps your code concise and lets the game engine manage the property state transitions natively.

### Gemini

Event classes in NeoForge act as listener hubs. They sit between Minecraft's engine and your custom code, intercepting gameplay actions as they happen across the world.

### Why You Need Event Classes for Blocks Like Hoppers

When a player right-clicks a container block like a hopper, chest, or furnace, Minecraft's default interaction chain executes in a strict order:

1. **Block First:** The engine asks the target block (`HopperBlock`) if it wants to handle the interaction.
2. **GUI Open:** Hoppers immediately handle right-clicks by opening their inventory GUI.
3. **Item Blocked:** Because the block handles the click, the engine stops the sequence right there. Your item's `useOn` method in `YoolItem` never gets called at all.

An event class listening to `PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock` intercepts the click at a higher priority level **before** the block can open its GUI. Calling `event.setCanceled(true)` cancels the default GUI opening and lets your Yool run its property cycling logic safely.

### Do You Need a Separate Class File?

You do not strictly need a brand-new file if you prefer to keep your codebase clean and compact. You can embed the event handler directly inside `YoolItem.java` as a static inner class or method:

```java
package com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.item.custom;

import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.ModBlocks;
import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.ModItems;
import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.PraeteritumFuturumMod;
import com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.block.entity.MachineFrameworkBlockEntity;
import net.minecraft.core.BlockPos;
import net.minecraft.sounds.SoundEvents;
import net.minecraft.sounds.SoundSource;
import net.minecraft.world.InteractionResult;
import net.minecraft.world.entity.player.Player;
import net.minecraft.world.item.Item;
import net.minecraft.world.item.ItemStack;
import net.minecraft.world.item.context.UseOnContext;
import net.minecraft.world.level.Level;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.Block;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.Blocks;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.HopperBlock;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.entity.BlockEntity;
import net.minecraft.world.level.block.state.BlockState;
import net.neoforged.bus.api.SubscribeEvent;
import net.neoforged.fml.common.EventBusSubscriber;
import net.neoforged.neoforge.event.entity.player.PlayerInteractEvent;
import org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull;

@EventBusSubscriber(modid = PraeteritumFuturumMod.MODID)
public class YoolItem extends Item {

    public YoolItem(Properties properties) {
        super(properties);
    }

    @Override
    public @NotNull InteractionResult useOn(@NotNull UseOnContext context) {
        Level level = context.getLevel();
        BlockPos pos = context.getClickedPos();
        Player player = context.getPlayer();

        if (player != null && player.isShiftKeyDown()) {
            if (!level.isClientSide) {
                BlockEntity blockEntity = level.getBlockEntity(pos);
                if (blockEntity instanceof MachineFrameworkBlockEntity) {
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.ITEM_FRAME_REMOVE_ITEM, SoundSource.BLOCKS, 1.0F, 1.0F);
                    Block.popResource(level, pos, new ItemStack(ModBlocks.MACHINE_FRAMEWORK.get().asItem()));
                    level.removeBlock(pos, false);
                    return InteractionResult.SUCCESS;
                }
            }
            return InteractionResult.SUCCESS;
        }

        return super.useOn(context);
    }

    @SubscribeEvent
    public static void onRightClickBlock(PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock event) {
        Player player = event.getEntity();
        ItemStack stack = player.getItemInHand(event.getHand());

        if (stack.is(ModItems.YOOL.get())) {
            Level level = event.getLevel();
            BlockPos pos = event.getPos();
            BlockState state = level.getBlockState(pos);

            if (state.is(Blocks.HOPPER)) {
                if (!level.isClientSide()) {
                    BlockState newState = state.cycle(HopperBlock.FACING);
                    level.setBlock(pos, newState, 3);
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), SoundSource.BLOCKS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
                }

                event.setCanceled(true);
                event.setCancellationResult(InteractionResult.SUCCESS);
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Will You Need Event Classes in the Future?

Yes, event classes are central to complex Minecraft modding whenever you need to override default game behaviors or respond to global events. Common use cases include:

- **Custom Drops:** Modifying block drops dynamically when broken under specific conditions.
- **Mob Interactions:** Changing entity behavior when hit by custom weapons or modules.
- **World Tick Operations:** Running scheduled background checks every game tick across the dimension.
- **Living Events:** Intercepting player damage, hunger, or movement calculations.

Keeping all tool logic inside `YoolItem.java` using `@EventBusSubscriber` gives you the best of both worlds: complete control over vanilla container block clicks without extra files crowding your project.

Yes, exactly.

Using the `@EventBusSubscriber` approach on `PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock` is the right strategy. Since containers like Droppers, Dispensers, and Chests open their own GUIs on right-click just like Hoppers do, standard item `useOn` calls get intercepted by vanilla block logic.

By handling this through the event subscriber, you can check if the clicked block has any rotatable block state property and cycle it directly before the block opens its interface.

Here is how you can expand the handler inside `YoolItem.java` to support any direction-based block:

```java
    @SubscribeEvent
    public static void onRightClickBlock(PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock event) {
        Player player = event.getEntity();
        ItemStack stack = player.getItemInHand(event.getHand());

        if (stack.is(ModItems.YOOL.get())) {
            Level level = event.getLevel();
            BlockPos pos = event.getPos();
            BlockState state = level.getBlockState(pos);

            // Handle Hoppers specifically (5 valid directions: down, north, south, west, east)
            if (state.is(Blocks.HOPPER)) {
                if (!level.isClientSide()) {
                    BlockState newState = state.cycle(HopperBlock.FACING);
                    level.setBlock(pos, newState, 3);
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), SoundSource.BLOCKS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
                }
                event.setCanceled(true);
                event.setCancellationResult(InteractionResult.SUCCESS);
                return;
            }

            // Generic support for standard 6-directional blocks (Droppers, Dispensers, Observers, Pistons)
            if (state.hasProperty(BlockStateProperties.FACING)) {
                if (!level.isClientSide()) {
                    BlockState newState = state.cycle(BlockStateProperties.FACING);
                    level.setBlock(pos, newState, 3);
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), SoundSource.BLOCKS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
                }
                event.setCanceled(true);
                event.setCancellationResult(InteractionResult.SUCCESS);
                return;
            }

            // Generic support for horizontal 4-directional blocks (Furnaces, Chests, Repeaters)
            if (state.hasProperty(BlockStateProperties.HORIZONTAL_FACING)) {
                if (!level.isClientSide()) {
                    BlockState newState = state.cycle(BlockStateProperties.HORIZONTAL_FACING);
                    level.setBlock(pos, newState, 3);
                    level.playSound(null, pos, SoundEvents.UI_BUTTON_CLICK.value(), SoundSource.BLOCKS, 0.5F, 1.0F);
                }
                event.setCanceled(true);
                event.setCancellationResult(InteractionResult.SUCCESS);
            }
        }
    }
```

### Why This Works so Well

- **`BlockStateProperties.FACING`**: Matches blocks like Droppers, Dispensers, Observers, and Pistons that rotate across all 6 directions (Up, Down, North, South, East, West).
- **`BlockStateProperties.HORIZONTAL_FACING`**: Matches blocks like Furnaces, Chests, and Blast Furnaces that only rotate on the horizontal plane.
- **Property Safety**: Calling `state.hasProperty(...)` prevents any crashes or invalid state assignments when interacting with non-rotatable blocks.

and now i have to register this bus thingie in here right?

### Gemini

Because you attached `@EventBusSubscriber(modid = PraeteritumFuturumMod.MODID)` directly above the `YoolInteractHandler` class definition, **you do not need to register it manually inside `PraeteritumFuturumMod.java`**.

NeoForge automatically scans your mod package at startup, finds the `@EventBusSubscriber` annotation, and registers its `@SubscribeEvent` methods to the main game event bus.

### How Event Registration Works in NeoForge

1. **Automatic Registration via Annotation:** Adding `@EventBusSubscriber(modid = PraeteritumFuturumMod.MODID)` tells NeoForge to hook up all `public static` methods marked with `@SubscribeEvent` to the **`NeoForge.EVENT_BUS`** automatically.
2. **The Mod Event Bus vs. Game Event Bus:**
  - **Mod Event Bus (`modEventBus` in `PraeteritumFuturumMod.java`):** Used for setup/lifecycle events like registering items, blocks, capabilities, and network payloads.
  - **Game Event Bus (`NeoForge.EVENT_BUS`):** Used for gameplay events like `PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock`, entity damage, or tick events. The `@EventBusSubscriber` annotation defaults to this bus automatically.

Everything is set up correctly. Once `YoolInteractHandler.java` exists with that annotation, NeoForge handles the event listening automatically without extra lines in `PraeteritumFuturumMod.java`.

Implementing this blueprint system relies on a few key architectural steps:

### 1. Data Storage via Data Components

Minecraft 1.21 uses a data component system. We can store a custom data structure on the blueprint item stack to hold:

- A list of installed modules with their slot indices.
- Individual configurations for each module, including filters and item types.
- Side IO port configurations for every slot.

### 2. Renaming the Blueprint

Players can rename the blueprint item easily using a vanilla anvil. Item stacks support custom display names natively through the item name component, meaning renamed blueprints keep their custom titles across inventories and tooltips automatically.

### 3. Capturing Data from a Machine

When a player right-clicks a configured machine framework with a blueprint, the interaction verifies that the block entity contains active modules. The system serializes the module inventory, IO configurations, and filter states directly into the blueprint item components, followed by a confirmation sound.

### 4. Applying Data to a Target Machine

When a player right-clicks an empty machine framework with a written blueprint, the system runs a verification check against the player inventory for the required modules. If the player holds all necessary modules, the system consumes them from the player inventory, populates the target machine slots, and restores all saved filter settings and IO port configurations.

This warning means that every time your code calls the `isItemAllowedByFilters()` method, the call is preceded by a logical negation operator (`!`).

### 1. Add the Helper Method to `FilterModuleItem.java`

Open `FilterModuleItem.java` and add a static method that handles checking adjacent filter modules around both the IO slot and the target inventory slot:

```java
    public static boolean isItemBlockedByFilters(MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity, int ioModuleSlot, int targetSlotIndex, ItemStack stack) {
        Level level = blockEntity.getLevel();
        if (level == null) return false;
        HolderLookup.Provider registries = level.registryAccess();

        int[] ioNeighbors = blockEntity.getAdjacentSlots(ioModuleSlot);
        for (int adj : ioNeighbors) {
            ItemStack moduleStack = blockEntity.getModuleHandler().getStackInSlot(adj);
            if (moduleStack.is(ModItems.FILTER_MODULE.get())) {
                if (!test(moduleStack, stack, registries)) {
                    return true; // Blocked by IO filter
                }
            }
        }

        int[] invNeighbors = blockEntity.getAdjacentSlots(targetSlotIndex);
        for (int adj : invNeighbors) {
            ItemStack moduleStack = blockEntity.getModuleHandler().getStackInSlot(adj);
            if (moduleStack.is(ModItems.FILTER_MODULE.get())) {
                if (!test(moduleStack, stack, registries)) {
                    return true; // Blocked by Inventory filter
                }
            }
        }

        return false;
    }
```

### 2. Update `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity.java`

Now you can remove the old `isItemAllowedByFilters` method from `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity` and replace the check inside `transferItems` to call the new method directly:

```java
    private void transferItems(IItemHandler source, IItemHandler target, int ioModuleSlot, int targetSlotIndex) {
        for (int i = 0; i < source.getSlots(); i++) {
            ItemStack extracted = source.extractItem(i, 1, true);

            if (!extracted.isEmpty()) {
                // Calls the filter check directly without inversion, clearing the IDE warning
                if (FilterModuleItem.isItemBlockedByFilters(this, ioModuleSlot, targetSlotIndex, extracted)) {
                    continue;
                }

                ItemStack remainder = extracted.copy();

                for (int j = 0; j < target.getSlots(); j++) {
                    remainder = target.insertItem(j, remainder, false);
                    if (remainder.isEmpty()) break;
                }

                int moved = extracted.getCount() - remainder.getCount();
                if (moved > 0) {
                    source.extractItem(i, moved, false);
                    setChanged();
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
    }
```

This delegates the filter evaluation logic to the filter item class, removes dead code from your block entity, and resolves the static analysis warning completely.

The IDE assumes that if a method returns a non-void object (like `ItemStack`), different implementations will eventually return actual item stacks. - Future modules (like advanced inventory modules, liquid tanks, or processing units) will override this method and return actual `ItemStack` instances when items are shift-clicked between slots.

If you want to clear the warning from your IDE analysis view, you can document the interface method with a Javadoc and add `@SuppressWarnings("SameReturnValue")` above the method signature:

```

In modular architecture, placing the logic inside **`FilterModuleItem`** (or calling `FilterModuleItem.isItemBlockedByFilters(...)` directly) is the cleanest design choice.

### Why this makes the most sense:

1. **Single Source of Truth:** `FilterModuleItem` owns the filtering rules (whitelist/blacklist logic, NBT/component evaluations, ghost slot matching). If you add new filter mechanics later, you only update `FilterModuleItem`.
2. **Decoupled Machine Framework:** `MachineFrameworkBlockEntity` coordinates module operations and item transfers, but it shouldn't need to implement the specifics of how individual modules filter items.

### The Clean Solution

#### Step 1: Update `IoModuleItem.java`

In `IoModuleItem.java`, inside `FilteredSingleSlotItemHandler`, change the check to call `FilterModuleItem` directly:

```java
public static class FilteredSingleSlotItemHandler extends com.thextrunner.praeteritum_futurum.inventory.SingleSlotItemHandler {
    private final MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity;
    private final int ioModuleSlot;
    private final int targetSlot;

    public FilteredSingleSlotItemHandler(net.neoforged.neoforge.items.IItemHandlerModifiable itemHandler, int slot, MachineFrameworkBlockEntity blockEntity, int ioModuleSlot) {
        super(itemHandler, slot);
        this.blockEntity = blockEntity;
        this.ioModuleSlot = ioModuleSlot;
        this.targetSlot = slot;
    }

    @Override
    public @NotNull ItemStack insertItem(int slot, @NotNull ItemStack stack, boolean simulate) {
        // Direct call to FilterModuleItem helper
        if (FilterModuleItem.isItemBlockedByFilters(blockEntity, ioModuleSlot, this.targetSlot, stack)) {
            return stack; // Rejected by filters!
        }
        return super.insertItem(slot, stack, simulate);
    }
}
```

    return !FilterModuleItem.isItemBlockedByFilters(this, ioModuleSlot, targetSlotIndex, stack);
}
```

### You

i have a question, why are some of my items initialized as <item> and others as <module name item>

### Gemini

The distinction between initializing items as `DeferredItem<Item>` versus specific subclass types like `DeferredItem<InventoryModuleItem>` comes down to **Java generics** and **compile-time type safety** within NeoForge’s registry system.

When you define a registry field using `DeferredItem<T>`, the generic parameter `T` dictates the exact Java class type returned when you call the `.get()` method on that registry object later in your code.

### 1. Generic `<Item>` Type Registration

Items such as `ANOMALY_COMPASS`, `SALVAGE_CUTTER`, `YOOL`, and `BLUEPRINT` are declared as `DeferredItem<Item>`:

- **Why it is used:** Even though these items use custom extension classes under the hood (such as `AnomalyCompassItem` or `BlueprintItem`), their registry wrapper is typed broadly as the base `Item` class.
- **Design implication:** You typically interact with these items through standard item stacks, tags, or registry comparisons (`itemStack.is(...)`), meaning you rarely need to call unique, custom Java methods directly on the registered item instance from an external class. Treating them as a generic `Item` keeps the variable references generalized and flexible.

### 2. Specific Subclass Type Registration (`InventoryModuleItem`, `IoModuleItem`, etc.)

Modules such as `INVENTORY_MODULE`, `IO_MODULE`, `FILTER_MODULE`, `SMELTING_MODULE`, `STONECUTTER_MODULE`, and `COMPOSTER_MODULE` are explicitly typed with their concrete custom classes (e.g., `DeferredItem<InventoryModuleItem>`):

- **Why it is used:** These specialized module classes contain unique, highly specific static helper methods, data component configuration handlers, client-side overlay renderers, and custom menu providers that your block entities or screen handlers need to reference directly.
- **Design implication:** By typing the `DeferredItem` wrapper with the specific subclass, calling `ModItems.IO_MODULE.get()` immediately returns an instance of `IoModuleItem` instead of a generic `Item`. This completely eliminates the need for manual type casting (e.g., `(IoModuleItem) item`) throughout your machine logic, network packets, and container screens, ensuring clean and type-safe code structure.

### You

why is it not resolving that property now

### Gemini

This error happens because you called `ITEMS.register(...)` instead of `ITEMS.registerItem(...)`.

In NeoForge:

- **`ITEMS.registerItem(name, supplier)`**: Expects a lambda taking `Item.Properties` as its argument (`properties -> new BlueprintItem(properties...)`).
- **`ITEMS.register(name, supplier)`**: Expects a generic supplier taking `ResourceLocation` as its argument, which causes Java to treat `properties` as a `ResourceLocation` instead of `Item.Properties`.

### The Fix

Change `ITEMS.register` to `ITEMS.registerItem` in `ModItems.java`:

```java
public static final DeferredItem<Item> BLUEPRINT =
        ITEMS.registerItem("blueprint",
                properties -> new BlueprintItem(properties.stacksTo(1))
        );
```

*Verification:* Once updated to `registerItem`, Java correctly resolves `properties` as `Item.Properties`, and the error on `stacksTo(1)` disappears.
